It buys that speed with two assumptions, that same-template lines share a token count and that early tokens are constants.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Normalisation: one event, one shape (ECS and OCSF)
md: A Windows 4625 converted to ECS and an sshd failure converted to ECS look identical to a rule, which is the point, but also a risk: a mapping mistake (say, putting the target host into source.ip) now breaks every rule at once. Test mappings with sample events from each source, exactly like rules (lesson 11).

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Baselines, anomalies and UEBA: how Storm-0558 was caught
md: State's advantage was not a product; it was three years of studying normal mailbox access, which let a modest-looking event stand out. The CSRB notes that buying the logs alone would not have been enough: few organisations analysed that voluminous log in detail.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Other routes to long context: base scaling, searched factors, data
md: Long data alone was not enough. Xiong et al. report that with Llama 2's original base the model still could not attend effectively beyond about 4,000 to 6,000 tokens after extensive long-context continual pretraining. Changing the base of a finished model without training, on the other hand, is just NTK-aware scaling with a huge s. The knob and the training go together.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Does the model use its context? Evaluation
md: Extending RoPE (PI, NTK, YaRN) makes long positions *in distribution*; Ring Attention and context parallelism make long sequences *fit*; neither guarantees the model *uses* the context. Measure effective length with depth-controlled tasks such as RULER.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Build it: loop your GPT with input injection and random depth
md: Everything here is one seed of a 219K-parameter model on a synthetic task. Treat the numbers as a demonstration of the mechanism (more iterations resolve deeper chains, exits track depth, starts are forgotten), not as evidence about which adapter is better at scale.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: LoRA: a frozen weight plus a trainable low-rank update
md: LoRA = frozen W0 + (alpha/r) B A, with B initialized to zero. You train r times (d + k) numbers per adapted matrix, and the model starts exactly at the pretrained one.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Exact unlearning: retraining without the data, made cheaper with SISA
md: Exact unlearning means the result is what retraining without the forget set would give. SISA keeps that guarantee by confining each point's influence to one shard and one suffix of slices, so only that part is retrained.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Hidden, not gone: relearning, probing and quantization attacks
md: Low scores on forget benchmarks show suppressed outputs, not erased knowledge. Small fine-tunes, probes and even 4-bit quantization can bring "forgotten" knowledge back, because approximate unlearning moves the weights only slightly.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: Notarization, revocation and the Shlayer lesson
md: Notarization means "Apple's automated scan found nothing known-bad when this was uploaded". It is not a review of intent, and it can be fooled by code that only turns malicious later or hides its payload. Its real strength is speed of revocation once something is reported.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: Case: Atomic Stealer and the paste-into-Terminal era
md: Resetting the user's password is not enough after a stealer. Session cookies stolen from the browser let the attacker into SaaS apps without the password or MFA until those sessions are revoked server-side.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: The PE format: headers, sections and what imports reveal
md: Our benign hello.exe imports VirtualProtect and VirtualQuery even though main never calls them: the MinGW-w64 C runtime's startup code uses them. One 'suspicious' import proves nothing. Read imports as a combination, and check what the compiler's runtime adds.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Writing and testing YARA rules
md: A YARA rule is a hypothesis about what makes a family unique. The test set is the evidence. Keep the test files and expected results next to the rule, and rerun them on every change, just like unit tests.

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: Storage math: dimensions times bytes per number
md: Savings multiply, but so do quality losses. Each step (fewer dims, fewer bits) costs some recall, and the costs compound. Measure recall on your own queries at the exact size and precision you plan to serve, then use a rerank stage (next lesson) to win most of it back.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, CP, MoE, FP8 and MFU
lessonTitle: Activation memory: sequence parallelism, selective recompute, CP
md: The 5as/h term assumes attention materializes the s x s score matrix. Fused attention kernels (FlashAttention, Dao et al. 2022, which computes attention tile by tile in fast on-chip memory; also in NVIDIA's Transformer Engine library) never store it, so most of that term disappears by itself. Megatron Core's config even warns that with fused attention there is no need to put core_attn in --recompute-modules.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, CP, MoE, FP8 and MFU
lessonTitle: Hands on: plan, launch, profile and checkpoint an MCore run
md: Plan with the formulas (state, activations, bubble), launch with flags that encode the plan, measure MFU against a named peak, profile for exposed communication and bubbles, and checkpoint in a format you can reshard.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Handles, mutexes, sockets and registry hives in memory
md: Every network row in memory names its owning process, and every handle names its holder. That pairing (this PID talked to that address, this PID opened that process) is what turns a list of artefacts into an attribution inside the host.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Size classes: buying speed with internal waste
md: `sizeof` is not what you pay. With a million 130-byte records you might budget 124 MiB, but jemalloc hands out 160 bytes each (153 MiB) and a power-of-two allocator 256 (244 MiB). Measure with `malloc_usable_size` or allocator stats, not by multiplying `sizeof`.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: Acquire and release: publishing data across threads
md: Synchronization needs a pair on the same atomic: a Release (or stronger) write and an Acquire (or stronger) read that observes that write or its release sequence. Then everything before the write is visible after the read.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: RCU: publish a new version, free the old after a grace period
md: RCU protects readers from updaters, not updaters from each other. `rcu_assign_pointer()` does not make two concurrent updates safe; the example still takes `foo_mutex`. And a pointer from `rcu_dereference()` is valid only inside the critical section that fetched it.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Heap overflow: corrupting the neighbouring object
md: A heap overflow damages whoever happens to be next, and you cannot predict who that is: it depends on the allocator, the sizes and the order of allocations. Treat any heap overflow as able to corrupt any nearby object.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Triplet loss: the margin and easy, semi-hard, hard negatives
md: Hard is not the same as useful. The very hardest negatives in a large dataset are often mislabeled or badly imaged examples (FaceNet names both). Training only on them teaches the network to fit noise.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: Warm caches in the benchmark, cold caches in production
md: A microbenchmark's working set and access pattern are part of the experiment. Report them next to the time, and sweep the size if the code's data can be large.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Launching and watching a Miles run
md: A Miles launch script is the recipe of record: read its options table and `EXEC:` lines to know what ran, override with `--extra-args` (the last flag wins), and keep lasting changes in the script. Judge the run against the monitoring table, telling a one-time jump in logprob diff from a climb.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Beyond GRPO: distillation, exact alignment and a 744B run
md: Bitwise-equal logprobs do not make an async run on-policy. True-on-policy alignment removes numerical mismatch between engines, not staleness from training on groups generated under older weights; the data buffer bounds that separately.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: Deploying learned policies: inference budgets, drift and guardrails
md: Reported speedups are relative to specific baselines on specific traces: B-LRU on six CDN traces, a tuned weighted fair scheduler on TPC-H mixes, a read-optimized B-tree on read-only integer keys. A different workload, or a stronger baseline, can shrink the gain to zero.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: Content providers and shared files: from URI grants to Dirty Stream
md: A shared file arrives with two attacker-controlled things: its content and its name. Treat both as untrusted input. Choose your own name, and parse the content as hostile.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Low-rank joint compression: cache one latent, rebuild every head
md: MLA is not a compression applied to an already trained model's cache, like PCA (principal component analysis, which finds the few directions that capture most of the variation in a set of vectors) run on stored keys. The down- and up-projections are ordinary weights learned from scratch during pretraining. Converting an existing MHA or GQA model to MLA needs extra fine-tuning work (see lesson 7).

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Merge, swap, or compute the adapter on the fly
md: Unmerged does not mean easy. Requests in one batch use adapters with different ranks and different sequence lengths, so padding everything into one batched matmul wastes work. S-LoRA's variant that copies adapters into contiguous memory and uses padded batched matmul (S-LoRA-bmm) was much slower than the version with custom kernels, GPU functions written for exactly this mixed-rank job.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Build it and size it: a mixed-adapter layer and a capacity plan
md: "Power-law popularity with exponent alpha" means different things in different papers. S-LoRA's alpha = 1 is uniform, Punica's Zipf-1.5 makes each adapter 1.5 times as popular as the next, and this lesson's Zipf exponent 1 gives the top adapter 14.7%. Compare results only after converting to the same quantity, such as the top-10 share.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: Drift, redundancy, reranker budgets, and when to skip it
md: Use multi-query when recall is the bottleneck because users word things differently from the corpus, and the next stage can absorb more candidates. Skip it for precise lookups, compound questions (decompose instead), tight latency budgets, and pipelines where a fixed reranker budget already decides the outcome. Measure end-to-end, not just first-stage recall.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: Why lookahead helps, and where it does not
md: These are intuitions, not proofs. The paper itself titles this section 'Why does it work? Some speculation'. Treat them as reasons MTP could help, then check the experiments.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Muon: orthogonalize the momentum with a few matrix multiplies
md: Muon does not produce an exactly orthogonal matrix. The reference implementation's docstring says the result is closer to $US'V^\top$ with the entries of $S'$ roughly uniform in $[0.5, 1.5]$, and that this does not hurt model performance. The Moonlight team also found 10 steps gave a more accurate result than 5 but no better training.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: Why the best learning rate drifts as models get wider
md: muTransfer has three steps: parametrize the target in muP, tune a smaller version of it, copy the tuned HPs to the target. It works because muP makes the optimal HPs converge to fixed values as width grows.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: muTransfer in practice: what transfers and what it saved
md: Don't expect dropout or weight decay tuned on a small proxy to be optimal for a much larger model trained on different amounts of data. The paper also notes that muTransfer may not be enough for fine-tuning on small datasets, where regularization matters most.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: When spinning wastes the CPU, and how much to spin
md: `spin_loop()` is not `yield` (such as Rust's `std::thread::yield_now()`, which asks the operating system scheduler to run another thread for now). It is a hint to the CPU, not to the scheduler: a thread spinning with it still occupies the CPU for its whole time slice.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Snapshots: how each transaction picks its version
md: Visibility is decided at read time by comparing tuple stamps against the reader's snapshot. Changing *when* the snapshot is taken changes what a transaction sees, without touching the data.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: The task: pull typed spans out of running text
md: An NER system is three pieces that must agree with each other: a **tag set** that can represent any set of non-overlapping spans, a **model** that scores tag sequences, and a **decoder** that turns tags back into spans. Most NER bugs live in the seams between them, not in the model.

courseTitle: Nation-state cyber operations and cyber conflict
lessonTitle: Who runs them: services, commands, contractors and fronts
md: A company named in an indictment is not proof that all of its work is state-directed, nor that a state ordered a particular intrusion. DOJ itself says i-Soon worked both on request and "on its own initiative", and that charges are allegations until proven in court.

courseTitle: Nation-state cyber operations and cyber conflict
lessonTitle: What the war showed, and what is still argued about
md: Both "cyber war turned out to be hype" and "cyber decided the war" overclaim. The public record is partial: most operations and most defensive successes are classified or unpublished. State which source a conclusion comes from, what data it rests on, and whether its author calls it a finding or a hypothesis.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: Write NSA and DSA as masked attention and test them against dense
md: Write the masked reference first. Setting the sparsity knob to select everything must reproduce dense attention exactly, and any fast kernel can then be compared with the reference on random inputs, including its gradients.

courseTitle: NeMo RL: NVIDIA's Ray-based post-training library
lessonTitle: One controller, many RL Actors: the NeMo RL architecture
md: NeMo RL separates *what the algorithm does* (a single-controller loop written as if on one GPU) from *where it runs* (RayVirtualCluster plus RayWorkerGroups). Swapping vLLM for another engine, or changing GPU counts, should not change the algorithm code.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: DHCP starvation and rogue DHCP servers
md: Whoever answers DHCP chooses a device's gateway and DNS server, so a rogue DHCP server is an on-path attack on every device it reaches. Only trusted ports may send DHCP server messages.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: Segmentation, zero trust and the Target breach
md: Segmentation limits how far one compromise spreads; zero trust removes network location as a reason to trust anything. Both assume a breach will happen, and both only pay off when someone watches the alerts at the boundaries.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: What TLS still reveals, and fingerprinting clients with JA3
md: A fingerprint identifies a TLS library and its configuration, not an intention. Python, Go and Windows programs share fingerprints with malware written in the same language or on the same stack. Use JA3 to cluster and to rank leads, never as a verdict on its own.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: From bits on a wire to packets
md: Every packet is a header plus a payload. Every device on the path must read the header to deliver it, and can read the payload too unless it is encrypted. Both facts drive almost everything in network security.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: HTTPS and TLS at a glance: what encryption hides and what it does not
md: TLS protects the content of one connection between two endpoints. It does not hide who talks to whom, it does not make the server trustworthy, and it does not protect data once it is decrypted at either end.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Memory policies: local, bind, preferred and interleave
md: Policy = mode + nodes + scope, applied at allocation time. Use bind for strict isolation, preferred when spilling over is acceptable, interleave for big shared data, and leave private per-thread data on the default local policy.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: What a detector outputs, and how two boxes are compared
md: A detector outputs a variable-size set of (box, class, score) triples, and IoU between boxes is the measure every later stage builds on.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Counting objects: by detection, by density, by tracking
md: Pick the counting method by scene: detection when objects are separable and you need locations, density maps for dense crowds where boxes fail, and tracking plus line or region events for video, where the same object appears in many frames.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: Counters, gauges, histograms, and the quantile you must not average
md: Never compute a rate as last value minus first value over a counter. One restart in the window turns a positive rate into a large negative number, and `rate()` exists precisely to handle that case for you.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Why OCR is a pipeline: find the text, then read it
md: OCR is a chain: detect, then recognize, then order and extract. Each stage only sees the previous stage's output, so an early error silently becomes a wrong field later.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: The kernel/user boundary: rings and the system call door
md: User programs run in ring 3 and can only ask; the kernel runs in ring 0 and decides. A system call is the only door between them. Sandboxing is mostly the art of closing doors and narrowing what each open door accepts.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: Sandboxes: Chrome's broker model, macOS and iOS
md: A broker is only as good as its request checking. A broker that performs "open this path" for any path a renderer names has turned itself into a tool for the attacker. That failure has a name, the confused deputy, and it is the subject of lesson 15.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Your own footprint while investigating: OPSEC and bias
md: Investigating leaves traces. Use a separate, logged-out research environment, expect the other side to read its logs, and record your exact queries because results differ by engine, location and history.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Geolocation: finding where a picture was taken
md: List clues, bound the area, eliminate candidates with the most distinctive clue first, then confirm with an independent feature. Report what matched and what could not be checked.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Putting it together: an ethical OSINT review, and where to practise
md: An ethical OSINT engagement is authorised, planned, minimal, preserved, verified and reported with its limits, and it ends with fixes and deleted working data.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: What CI does when you open a pull request
md: CI is a contract written in the repo: on these events, on these machines, run these commands, and block the merge unless they exit with status 0. Read `.github/workflows/` before your first PR to a project.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: What a reviewer is deciding: the code-health standard
md: Misconception: a reviewer who leaves 15 comments is blocking you on all 15. Often most are optional. If the reviewer did not say which ones block the merge, ask instead of guessing.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: Where a project's rules live and how GitHub finds them
md: Read in this order before you touch code: LICENSE (can you contribute at all), CONTRIBUTING (how), CODE_OF_CONDUCT (how to behave), SECURITY (if your finding is a vulnerability). Ten minutes of reading avoids a rejected PR.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Keeping a branch current: rebase onto upstream/main
md: Rebase rewrites history. The rule from Pro Git, the free Git book on git-scm.com: do not rebase commits that exist outside your repository and that people may have based work on. Your own PR branch is the usual exception, which is why the next lesson's force-push needs care, not a ban.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: No license means no permission: what a license grants
md: Public is not the same as open source. Code you can read on GitHub with no license file is all rights reserved, and so is a snippet whose license you never checked.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: The DCO: certifying every commit with Signed-off-by
md: CLA: one signed agreement per person or company, granting rights up front. DCO: no agreement, just a per-commit certification of origin via Signed-off-by, checked mechanically by email match.

courseTitle: Reading a large codebase: search, trace and dig through history
lessonTitle: Map the repository before you read a line of it
md: A common mistake is to fix a bug inside a generated file. Your edit is overwritten the next time the generator runs, and reviewers will reject it. When a file says *do not edit*, find its input (here `src/commands/get.json`) in the build rule and change that instead.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: Shrinking a failing program by hand
md: Every cut is an experiment: remove, rerun, compare to the original failure. Keep cuts that preserve the exact error; undo the rest.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: One logical change per PR, and every commit builds
md: If the project squash-merges PRs, your intermediate commits disappear from the main branch anyway, and the PR as a whole becomes one commit. That makes **one logical change per PR** even more important: the squash cannot separate a fix from a speedup after the fact.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Block tables: virtual memory for the KV cache
md: Paging is not free. The paper measured 20 to 26% higher attention kernel latency than FasterTransformer's kernel, from block-table lookups, extra branches and variable lengths (the next lesson shows where those come from). It still wins end to end because only the attention operator pays, and the larger batch more than makes up for it.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, and when caching pays
md: Longest-prefix-first can starve a request whose prefix is never cached, since others keep jumping ahead. The SGLang paper says so and leaves fair scheduling as future work.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Passive recon: certificate logs, search engines and leaked code
md: A leaked password or API key found during recon is not an invitation to log in with it. Unless the rules of engagement explicitly allow using discovered credentials, record where it was found and report it at once so it can be rotated.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: Reading a flame graph: width, top edges and plateaus
md: Colors carry no meaning in a default CPU flame graph. Gregg picks random warm colors only to separate neighbors. Other palettes exist (for example coloring kernel, user and just-in-time (JIT) frames differently, where JIT code is machine code that a runtime such as the Java virtual machine compiles while the program runs), but never read hotness from hue.

courseTitle: Persistent memory data structures: crash consistency per cache line
lessonTitle: Flushes, fences and the order things become durable
md: A fence without a flush does nothing for durability on ADR platforms, and a flush without a fence gives no ordering: CLWB and CLFLUSHOPT are not ordered with each other or with later stores. You need both, in the order store, flush, fence, then the dependent store.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: DMARC: alignment, policy and reports
md: Misconception: "we have DMARC, so we are protected from phishing". DMARC at p=reject stops exact-domain spoofing of **your** domain. It does nothing against lookalike domains, display-name spoofs or a compromised real mailbox, and p=none stops nothing at all; it only reports.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: Shrinking a struct by reordering its fields
md: Do not reorder blindly. If a struct's layout is part of a file format, a network protocol, a hardware register map or an ABI shared with other code, changing the order changes the bytes and breaks every reader. Reordering is safe only for structs that are private to one build of your program.

courseTitle: Pose estimation: heatmaps, grouping, OKS and joint angles
lessonTitle: Heatmaps: training targets, argmax and sub-pixel decoding
md: The network never outputs coordinates. It outputs heatmaps, and a small hand-written decoder (argmax, quarter-cell shift, scale by stride, undo the crop) turns them into numbers. Bugs in that decoder, such as swapping x and y or forgetting the crop offset, look like a bad model.

courseTitle: Post-quantum cryptography and migration
lessonTitle: Encrypting one bit with LWE, by hand
md: This toy exists to make the math visible. Never write your own lattice cryptography for real use: use ML-KEM from a maintained library (lesson 8), whose implementers also handle constant-time code, input checks and randomness.

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Filtering inside the graph walk, and when the graph falls apart
md: Do not read 3% as a safe threshold. Proximity graphs are not random graphs, matching nodes are often clustered, and being connected is weaker than being *navigable*: greedy search can stall in a matching region long before the subgraph formally splits. Qdrant's docs simply warn that the HNSW graph starts to fall apart when filters are too strict.

courseTitle: Prefetching, memory bandwidth versus latency
lessonTitle: Latency versus bandwidth: two different walls
md: Common misconception: "faster RAM will speed up my tree or hash-chain lookups." Faster transfer rates raise peak bandwidth, but a dependent chain of misses uses a tiny fraction of it. Its cost is set by latency, which has improved far more slowly.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Pseudonyms and hashes are not anonymity: AOL 2006
md: Pseudonyms protect the name, not the person. They link all of one person's records, and those records (queries, routes, purchases) can identify them by content. Ask what a released record says, not only what field was deleted.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Differential privacy: a promise about one person
md: Differential privacy is a property of the mechanism: on any two datasets differing in one person, every output is at most e^epsilon times likelier on one than the other. It survives post-processing and any auxiliary data, and epsilons add up across releases.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Designing for less: data minimisation and purpose limitation
md: Minimise by architecture: collect less, coarsen at the edge, compute on the device, separate identity from content, enforce purposes in the access layer and in database grants, and default to the least sharing.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Rights in code: access and erasure across every copy
md: Rights are requirements on every copy: build a data map (system, lookup key, export method, erase method), meet the one-month clock (Art. 12(3)), put backups beyond use, notify recipients, and verify identity in proportion to what you would hand over.

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: Defending the path: segmentation, admin hygiene, EDR, HSE timeline
md: Escalation and lateral movement are a chain of small, valid-looking steps. Make each step harder (least privilege, unique and protected credentials, segmentation, patching known-exploited bugs) and make each step visible (forwarded logs, EDR, the event chains in this course), then make sure every alert has an owner.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Using a PRM: reranking, step-level search and RL
md: Same scores, three uses: rerank finished solutions (weighted voting is a strong default), prune partial solutions in beam search (best on harder problems at modest budgets), or provide step-level rewards so RL can credit each step separately.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: Who runs next: run queues, CFS, EEVDF and nice
md: Misconception: "nice 19 means it only runs when the machine is idle." A nice 19 task still has weight 15, so against one nice 0 task it gets about 1.4 percent. For truly leftover CPU, use the `SCHED_IDLE` policy, which the CFS document describes as even weaker than nice 19.

courseTitle: Product quantization (PQ)
lessonTitle: Write PQ from scratch in numpy, then check it against Faiss
md: ADC is a gather plus a sum: `lut[np.arange(m), codes].sum(1)`. Once that clicks, every fast PQ kernel is the same loop made cheaper: smaller tables (lesson 7), fewer codes scanned (lesson 5) or better codes (lessons 6 and 9).

courseTitle: Automatic prompt optimization: APE, OPRO and DSPy
lessonTitle: DSPy: signatures, modules and optimizers
md: Every bootstrap and search optimizer trusts the metric. The DSPy docs warn that a non-deterministic metric (for example an LLM judge) makes the chosen demos "a function of metric noise as much as program quality". Make the metric deterministic where you can, validate any LLM judge against humans first, and keep a held-out set.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Why security teams script, and your first Python program
md: A script is the steps you would do by hand, written down once so they run the same way on every line. Its biggest risk is not crashing; it is quietly counting the wrong thing.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Hashing files and checking them against known-bad lists
md: Hash files in binary chunks, normalize every indicator to lowercase before comparing, and remember that a match means "known bad" while a miss means only "not this exact file".

courseTitle: Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites
lessonTitle: Synonym filters in Elasticsearch and OpenSearch
md: Create the synonym set before the index that references it. Elastic's guide warns that an index pointing at a missing set becomes inoperable and must be deleted and re-created, or closed and re-opened.

courseTitle: Query rewriting and decomposition
lessonTitle: Conversational rewriting: turning a follow-up into a standalone query
md: Misconception: the rewriter should make the query richer. Its job is to make it *standalone and faithful*. A rewriter that adds guessed facts (say, "when the leader fails during a network partition") can steer retrieval toward documents the user never asked about. Instruct it not to answer, and to return the message unchanged when it is already standalone.

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: Computing the estimate with popcount, and re-ranking by the bound
md: Per vector, the query-time work is a few AND plus popcount passes over the D-bit code and a handful of multiply-adds with precomputed factors. The error bound then tells you which candidates are worth an exact distance.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Prices, quantities and negative numbers: validating what input means
md: If a value influences price, access, ownership or state, assume the client made it up. Recompute it from server data, and validate every remaining input for business meaning: range, type, and how it combines with the other fields.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Case: Flexcoin and Poloniex, the bitcoin banks that raced (2014)
md: Internal balances are money. A transfer between two users of the same service can drain the service if the debit is not atomic, because every later withdrawal trusts those balances.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Testing logic: invariants, abuse cases and concurrency tests
md: A concurrency test that passes once proves little: races are probabilistic. Use many parallel workers, a barrier so they start together, a real database rather than a mock, and run it on every build so a later refactor that reopens the window is caught.

courseTitle: Retrieval-augmented generation: the pipeline and its failures
lessonTitle: Why an LLM needs a retriever: parametric vs non-parametric memory
md: RAG splits knowledge in two: the index decides **what facts are available**, the LLM decides **how they are read and phrased**. Every quality problem in this course is a failure of one of these two halves, or of the hand-off between them.

courseTitle: Feature engineering for ranking
lessonTitle: Normalization and missing values
md: Filling a missing value with 0 is safe only when 0 already means the worst value. For a feature like 1/window it does. For a z-scored feature, 0 means average, so a missing value silently becomes an average document. Use the worst observed value (LETOR's MIN approach) or add a separate is-missing flag.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: A crime with a supply chain: the roles and the money
md: Ransomware is a business whose only income is victims who pay. Every victim who can restore without paying lowers the expected value of the next intrusion, and every payment funds it.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: Backups that survive an attacker with Domain Admin
md: A backup survives only if the credentials, network and storage that protect it are independent of production identity. Keep at least one copy immutable in a separate account or offline, back up AD and the rebuild tooling too, and time real restores.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Scaling RDMA: NIC caches, doorbells, timeouts and failure
md: A short timeout detects dead peers fast but turns a transient congestion spike into a fatal QP error; a long one can stall an application for seconds. Pick it from your fabric's real round-trip and queueing delays, not from habit.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: Delta-encoded state and choosing the transport
md: Bandwidth is set by what changes, how it is encoded, and how often you send it. Latency under loss is set by the transport: an ordered stream turns one lost packet into a stall for every later update.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Evaluating recommenders without fooling yourself
md: A gap between a random-split number and a temporal-split number is not a bug in either; they measure different tasks. Only the temporal one resembles what the system will face, so compare models on that.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: Aggregation and sorting: running state, hash tables and spills
md: Aggregation keeps a small state per group. Hashing finds the state with a table (memory grows with groups); sorting brings each group together so one state suffices (needs ordered input). Sort and hash nodes both spill to disk when they exceed their memory limit.

courseTitle: Replication and quorums: N, R, W and what they really buy you
lessonTitle: Concurrent writes, conflict resolution and what quorums do not promise
md: Pick the knobs by the question each one answers: **N** sets how many copies survive, **W** how many machines must hold a write before "ok", **R** how many you ask on a read, and **the conflict rule** decides what happens when copies disagree. Real configs: Dynamo's common (N, R, W) of (3, 2, 2); R = 1, W = N for read-heavy catalogs; Cassandra QUORUM with QUORUM.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: When the verifier is code: test hacking in coding agents
md: Misconception: verifiable rewards cannot be hacked. A verifier is only as strong as its isolation. If the agent can write to the tests, the test runner, the libraries they import, or read the reference answer, *pass the tests* and *solve the task* come apart.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Assessing risk in practice: from asset list to risk register
md: An auditor asking about risk management wants to see: a documented method (scales, appetite), a register with named owners, dated decisions by people with the authority to make them, and evidence that the register is reviewed on schedule. A register nobody reviews fails the audit even if every score is right.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: NIST CSF 2.0: six functions, profiles and tiers
md: CSF 2.0: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover; 22 categories, 106 subcategories; current and target profiles define your roadmap; tiers describe rigour. Voluntary, outcome-based and free, which makes it the common language between engineers, executives and other frameworks.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: EU law for engineers: GDPR, NIS2, DORA and the Cyber Resilience Act
md: Notification duties stack. One ransomware incident at a cloud provider in Germany can mean a GDPR notification to the data protection authority (72 hours), a NIS2 early warning to the CSIRT (24 hours), DORA reports via financial customers, and contractual notices to customers. Decide in advance who files which report; the clocks start whether or not you have a plan.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Accountability: what boards, CISOs and engineers have answered for
md: Red flags that should make any engineer escalate in writing: being asked to delete or delay logs, to describe an intrusion as "research", to pay an attacker through a bug bounty, to tell a regulator or customer something you know is false, or to keep the general counsel or board out of the loop. Follow your company's whistleblowing or escalation path; your own integrity is the control.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Weight sync: resharding and moving the bytes every step
md: After new weights land, cached KV entries are wrong: they were computed by the old weights. SGLang's `update_weights_from_distributed` flushes the cache by default, and AReaL's interruptible workers discard KV caches and recompute them with the new weights before continuing unfinished sequences.

courseTitle: Roofline model and GPU bandwidth measurement
lessonTitle: Measuring achieved bandwidth with a copy kernel
md:
Common traps:
- **Arrays that fit in L2.** An 8 MB array on an H100 (50 MB L2) measures cache bandwidth, not HBM.
- **Mixing GB and GiB.** 2,982.6 GB/s is 2,777.8 GiB/s. Use one divisor for both theory and measurement.
- **Timing the first launch** or using host timers without synchronizing.
- **Uncoalesced or strided access**, which measures your access pattern, not the memory.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: Why fuse ranks instead of scores
md: RRF needs only positions. Scores on different scales, scores that drift between index versions, even systems that expose no scores at all can be fused, because $1/(k + r)$ is the same function of rank for every input.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: Fuse, tune and test RRF on real SciFact runs
md: Fusion tuning workflow: fix W for the next stage, choose parameters on a train split only, evaluate the chosen setting on held-out queries once, and report the difference with a paired test. In this SciFact run, RRF's default k = 60 was within noise of every tuned variant, while min-max CombSUM and CombMNZ beat it on both train and test (test p = 0.03 and 0.001).

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Intrusive lists, work items and condition variables
md: Misconception: "`wait` returns only after `notify`, so an `if` is enough." The CondVar docs say a wait may also wake spuriously, and with `notify_all` another waiter may have consumed the result first. Re-check the condition in a `while` loop every time `wait` returns.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: The scheduling cycle: select_cpu, enqueue, dispatch, run
md: Where a task finally runs is decided when it lands in a local DSQ, usually inside `ops.dispatch()` on the CPU that is asking for work. `select_cpu` is an optimization: matching the final CPU saves a bit of work, and picking an idle CPU wakes it up.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Keeping tasks in BPF: custody, dequeue and user-space policy
md: If you hold a task anywhere other than a terminal DSQ, implement `ops.dequeue()` and drop your reference there. The kernel will re-enqueue the task after any property change, so a stale entry means a task is queued twice.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: How secret scanners find keys: patterns, entropy, verification
md: A scanner finds only what looks like a secret. A custom token with no prefix, a password of ordinary words, or a key split across two lines passes silently. If you issue tokens yourself, copy GitHub's design: a unique prefix and a checksum make your secrets findable by every scanner and cheap to validate.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: What a secure code reviewer is looking for
md: Review the flow, not the line: find each source, follow it to each sink, and check the control (validation, encoding, authorization) at each step. Then ask what the code assumes and whether an attacker can make that assumption false.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Regular expressions that hang: ReDoS and the Cloudflare outage
md: A backtracking regex is safe only if every string has few ways to match it. Nested quantifiers and adjacent .* make the number of ways explode, so a short input can take seconds. Rewrite, bound the input, or use a linear-time engine.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Rust: FFI boundaries, release-mode overflow and panics
md: Rust review checklist beyond unsafe: arithmetic on input uses checked_* or try_from, not + or as; every FFI call has a SAFETY comment covering NUL termination, pointer lifetime, ownership and lengths; and no unwrap, expect or unchecked index on anything an attacker controls.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: IPsec traps: weak PSKs, aggressive mode, NULL and old algorithms
md: IKEv2 does not make a weak PSK safe. A client that connects to a rogue gateway (for example on hostile Wi-Fi with a spoofed address) completes IKE_SA_INIT with the rogue and sends its own AUTH to it. RFC 7296 states that dictionary attacks on user-chosen PSKs "are not prevented in this authentication method". Strong random PSKs, or certificates, are the fix.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Bell-LaPadula: no read up, no write down
md: Bell-LaPadula protects secrecy only. Writing up is allowed, so a low-level process may overwrite a TOP SECRET file it cannot read. Nothing in the model protects the integrity of data; that needs a different model, next lesson.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: The trust algorithm: criteria, scores and context
md: A score hides which factor failed. If a control must always hold (a patched OS for admin consoles, phishing-resistant MFA for payroll), make it a criterion, not a weight that other good signals can outvote.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: Idempotent steps: designing work that is safe to run twice
md: Derive the key from the event, let the database or the API enforce it atomically, and reuse the same key on every retry. Then duplicates from webhooks, queues and retries all collapse into one effect.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: When not to automate, and a design review checklist
md: Automate what is reversible, small and precisely triggered; cap and approve what attackers can trigger; keep irreversible, wide-impact and judgement-heavy steps with people; and give language models advice to write, never authority to act.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: How a vulnerability becomes public: disclosure, CVE and NVD
md: Path of a vulnerability: found, reported, fixed, numbered (CVE via a CNA), published with a patch, enriched by NVD (CVSS, CWE, products), patched by users. Attackers can enter at any point; the gap between patch release and patch install is where most damage happens.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Who does security work: the job families
md: Five families: offence, defence (SOC, detection, IR), AppSec, cloud security and GRC. They need the same foundations this track teaches: how systems work, how attacks work, and how to read, script and explain.

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: From gaps to a roadmap: strategy, sequencing and dependencies
md: A strategy is a diagnosis, a choice (including what you will not do) and coordinated actions. A roadmap places those actions by dependency and capacity, with an owner and a measurable outcome for each item. Re-plan it every quarter and show the board what is unfunded.

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: Hiring and keeping people: what predicts performance
md: Hire with work samples and structured, independently scored interviews; do not filter on years of experience or credentials the job does not need. Keep people with growth paths, sustainable on-call and time to learn.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Plain, direct and first: sentences a busy reader acts on
md: Hedging is not the same as honesty. "May potentially" hides uncertainty instead of stating it. If you are unsure, say what you know, what you do not, and how sure you are (the incident lesson later in this course gives you the words). If you are sure, do not hedge to sound modest.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Why a model can teach itself: improve, then distill
md: The search policy is a better policy than the network that guided it. Training the network to imitate it is **policy improvement by imitation**. No human labels are used, but new information does enter the loop: from look-ahead, and from the game rules that score every finished game.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Using failures and training the judge: V-STaR, the gap, Meta-Rewarding
md: Training the judge on its own meta-judgments imports new biases. By iteration 2 the meta-judge preferred the judgment with the higher score 97.68% of the time, the judge's mean score rose from 4.1 to over 4.7 out of 5, and position bias grew. Scores bunched near the top, which made responses harder to tell apart. Lesson 6 flagged the same risk: a judge's blind spots become the policy's target.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: Prompt compression: self-information, perplexity and Selective Context
md: Compression has costs of its own. The compressor runs on the critical path of every request. The compressed text is hard for humans to read, which makes debugging and audits harder. Exact strings (code, JSON, numbers, IDs) can be damaged by token deletion. And question-aware compression produces a different context for every question, so that context can no longer be served from the provider's prefix cache.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Log4Shell: how logging a string ran code
md: Log4Shell is injection in a place nobody thought was an interpreter. Logging user input is normal and correct; the library silently treated part of that input as template syntax with network access. Recall the injection course: whenever data is evaluated, the evaluator is the attack surface.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Cache-aware scheduling: queue order sets the hit rate
md: Greedy longest-prefix-first can **starve** a request whose prefix is never cached: requests that hit keep jumping ahead of it. The paper says so directly and leaves fair cache-aware scheduling as future work. Watch tail latency (the latency of the slowest requests, such as the 99th percentile) if you enable `lpm`.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: A*: steering the search with a lower bound
md: In practice the straight-line bound is weak on real road networks with travel times: it must divide by the top motorway speed, so it badly underestimates slow city streets. The Bast et al. survey reports the gain is small or nonexistent. **ALT** gets much better bounds from precomputed distances to a few landmarks plus the triangle inequality.

courseTitle: Signal processing basics: sampling, the FFT and filters
lessonTitle: The FFT: from N squared to N log N with butterflies
md: The FFT is not an approximation. It returns the same numbers as the DFT matrix product, up to floating point rounding, by sharing work through $\log_2 N$ stages of $N/2$ butterflies.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Arm Neon and SVE: fixed width versus length agnostic
md: Misconception: "SVE code is written for a particular width like 512 bits." VLA code must never assume a length; use svcntw() and whilelt. ACLE warns that something like `svptrue_pat_b32(SV_VL16)` loads no data at all on chips narrower than 512 bits.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: How Linux stacks them, and how to choose
md: A pool or arena that never returns memory looks like a leak from the outside. Bonwick's caches give memory back under memory pressure, when the virtual memory system runs short of free pages; your custom pool should have some way to shrink (reset, trim, or a size cap).

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Generating data: the rollout loop and your own functions
md: Put per-sample agent logic in a custom generate function and scoring in a custom reward function. You keep slime's batching, dynamic sampling, abort and partial-rollout machinery for free, and your code works unchanged under fully async rollout.

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: What a blockchain is: a shared ledger that nobody owns
md: "Private" is not secret. The Solidity docs warn that "everything you use in a smart contract is publicly visible, even local variables and state variables marked private". Every node stores the full state, so never put passwords, keys or unrevealed answers in a contract.

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: Unchecked external calls and denial of service
md: Do not "fix" the push auction by ignoring the refund's result. Then the refusing bidder's 10 ETH is silently kept by the auction while the books say it was refunded: you have traded a DoS for an accounting bug.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Verdicts, severity and priority: true, false and benign positives
md: Using a rule's historical precision in priority has a trap: a rule that is usually wrong will sink to the bottom forever, including the one time it is right. Precision should make you fix the rule, not ignore it. Target's "malware.binary" alerts are the cautionary tale.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Pivoting, building a timeline, and mapping it to ATT&CK
md: Do not force-fit. If you cannot say which technique an event shows, write the plain fact and leave the ID out. A wrong mapping in a case note propagates into reports and detection gap analyses.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Voice clones and deepfake meetings: when seeing is not believing
md: Misconception: "train people to spot deepfakes". Spotting artefacts is a losing race as tools improve, and the IC3 itself says AI content is often hard to identify. Teach the artefacts as a reason to pause, but make the decision depend on an independent channel.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Why single neurons are hard to read: superposition
md: Superposition: a layer with $d$ dimensions can represent many more than $d$ sparse features as almost-orthogonal directions, at the cost of interference. Neurons then mix many features, so we look for directions instead.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Reading a latent: activating examples, logit effects, autointerp
md: A Neuronpedia label is an LLM's guess from a sample of examples, not ground truth. Before you build on a latent, read examples from its lower activation intervals and a few non-activating contexts that seem to match the name.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Inverse distance weighting: weights from distance alone
md: IDW ignores how sensors sit relative to each other. S1 and S2 are only 2.24 km apart and both read 11, so they carry nearly the same information. IDW still counts both at full weight. If ten sensors sat in one parking lot, IDW would let that lot outvote everything else. Kriging, later in the course, fixes this.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Why decoding is slow and why checking guesses is cheap
md: Decoding is slow because each step moves all the weights to produce one token. Checking $K$ guessed tokens in one target pass moves the weights once, so every accepted guess is a target step you did not pay for.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Speculation in a serving system: batch size, long context and tuning
md: Speculation spends spare compute to save sequential steps. At small batch or long context the verify pass rides on memory reads that happen anyway; once $B(\gamma + 1)$ token rows reach the ridge, every rejected draft costs real time. Shrink $\gamma$ under load, and judge by ITL at fixed load, not by acceptance alone.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: The map of a process: segments, /proc/PID/maps and ASLR
md: A big line in `/proc/PID/maps` is not memory in use. A VMA only says which addresses the program may touch; Linux's memory concepts docs note that anonymous mappings usually just define those areas, and physical pages arrive on first access. A 1 GiB mapping that was never written uses almost no RAM.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: Walking an x86-64 page table, bit by bit
md: A miss does not always cost four DRAM reads. The page-table entries are ordinary data that can sit in the CPU caches, and Linux's page-table docs note that MMUs also keep page walk caches for upper levels. The four loads are the worst case of the structure, not a fixed latency.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Steering by adding a vector to the residual stream
md: A steering vector edits **activations**, not weights and not the prompt. It is computed once, before inference, and the same vector is added on every forward pass while it is switched on.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Ingest: MQTT at the edge, a Kafka log in the middle
md: Per-partition order is *write* order, not event-time order. If sensor A's readings were written late (e12 in our toy), they sit in the log after newer ones. Kafka removes the network chaos between bridge and processor, but it cannot undo disorder that happened before the write.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Why recurrence was the bottleneck for sequence models
md: Attention did not start with the Transformer. Additive attention over RNN states dates to Bahdanau et al. (2014). What was new in 2017 was using attention *alone*, with no recurrence or convolution.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Relative positions: from sinusoids to RoPE and ALiBi
md: Relative schemes put the offset m - n into the score itself. RoPE rotates queries and keys so their dot product depends only on content and offset; ALiBi subtracts a fixed per-head penalty proportional to distance. Neither adds anything to the input embeddings.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: Document length normalization: what b controls
md: b = 1 is not "more correct". It assumes every long document is just verbose. For collections where long documents genuinely cover more (manuals, books split into chapters), strong normalization buries them. The survey reports that values around 0.5 < b < 0.8 work well in many settings, with optimal values depending on the documents and queries.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Next-token prediction: turning raw text into training examples
md: `block_size` is the **maximum** context, not the only context. Because position $t$ in each chunk sees only $t+1$ tokens, the model is trained on every context length from 1 to `block_size`, which is exactly what it needs when generation starts from a short prompt.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Generating text: the sampling loop, temperature, top-k and top-p
md: Training scores all positions in parallel with teacher forcing; generation is a sequential loop over the same network that samples from the last position's distribution, shaped by temperature, top-k or top-p.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Many inputs: partial derivatives and the gradient vector
md: Steepest descent is a local statement. $-\nabla f(2, 1) = (-4, -6)$ does not point at the minimum $(0, 0)$, which lies in direction $(-2, -1)$. In an elongated bowl the gradient mostly points across the narrow valley, which is why plain gradient descent (repeatedly stepping against the gradient, lesson 6) zig-zags.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Files, paths and permissions: finding your way around
md: `rm` and `mv` act at once and say nothing. `mv` onto an existing name silently replaces that file, and `rm -r` cannot be undone. Before deleting with a pattern, run `ls` with the same pattern to see what it matches, and add `-i` to make `rm` or `mv` ask first.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Pipes: concurrent processes, sort | uniq -c, and SIGPIPE
md: A pipeline is several processes running concurrently and connected by bounded kernel buffers. Fast writers block on a full pipe; writers to a closed pipe get SIGPIPE. Tools like `sort` that need all their input are where a pipeline stops streaming.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Your environment and remote machines: dotfiles, ssh and tmux
md: The private key works like your password on every server that lists its public key. Never copy it to a server or commit it to a repository, and protect it with a passphrase; `ssh-agent` can hold the unlocked key so you type the passphrase once per session.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Embeddings for IDs: categorical features, hashing and weight tying
md: An ID embedding is trained by whatever loss it feeds. Supervised losses place IDs with similar effects on the target close together. When the ID space is huge or open, trade exactness for a fixed-size table: hash, share an unknown row, or build vectors from features.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Fewer bytes per weight: number formats and weight-only quantization
md: Quality loss depends on the model, the task and the method. gpt-fast saw no perceptible loss from INT8 weights but a measurable one at INT4, and Databricks warns that naive quantization can degrade quality substantially. Measure perplexity and a downstream task before shipping.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Measure it: tokens per second, MBU and MFU
md: Common timing mistakes: reading the clock without `torch.cuda.synchronize()` (you time the launch, not the work); including the first call (allocation and compilation); comparing tokens/s across different prompt lengths, output lengths or batch sizes; forgetting power and clock limits (gpt-fast's A100 was capped at 330 W). The *Microbenchmarking pitfalls* course covers the general rules.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Decisions in machine code: flags, compare and conditional jumps
md: An `if` is a compare that sets flags plus a conditional jump that reads them. Signed and unsigned comparisons differ only in which flags the jump reads: SF and OF for signed (jl, jg), CF for unsigned (jb, ja).

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: The OS in charge: system calls and sharing the CPU
md: The OS is not running alongside your program; it runs only when something hands it the CPU: a system call (the program asks), an exception (the program did something illegal), or an interrupt (hardware such as the timer or the disk demands attention).

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Reward models: turning human comparisons into a score
md: A reward model is a learned approximation, not ground truth. Stiennon et al. (2020), an OpenAI paper that used RLHF to summarize Reddit posts, found their reward model preferred longer summaries, and it can be confidently wrong on responses unlike its training data. Lesson 9 shows what happens when RL optimizes hard against such a model.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Building the index: tokens, sorting and postings
md: Whatever normalization you apply at index time (lowercasing, stemming, stripping punctuation) you must apply identically to queries. If the index stores `cache` and the query parser passes `Cache` through unchanged, the dictionary lookup finds nothing.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: TF-IDF: weighting by frequency and rarity
md: The base of the log in idf does not change the ranking: switching from log10 to ln multiplies every idf by the same constant (about 2.303), so every score scales equally. What does matter is the shape, for example whether tf is raw or sublinear.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: From main.c to a running program: the four toolchain stages
md: A header declaring a function is not the same as the function existing. `#include` only pastes a promise into your file. If the definition lives in `area.c` (or a library), it must also reach the linker, or the build fails at link time with an undefined symbol error even though every file compiled cleanly.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Integer types and conversions: where -1 > 0u
md: Never compare a signed value with an unsigned one without thinking about negatives. `if (len < cap)` with `int len = -1` and `size_t cap = 16` is false on LP64 systems: len converts to a huge size_t. Keep lengths and indexes in size_t throughout, or check for negatives before comparing.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Files and errors: stdio, return codes and errno
md: Do not test errno to find out whether a call failed. A successful call may leave errno nonzero from some earlier, unrelated failure, or even set it itself. Test the return value; consult errno only after the return value reports failure.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Who frees this memory? Ownership and drop
md: Ownership is not about the stack versus the heap as such. A `String` header can live on the stack, in a `Vec` (Rust's growable array), or inside a struct field; wherever it lives, that location is the owner, and the heap block is freed when that owner is dropped.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Structs that borrow: lifetimes in types and what 'static means
md: `T: 'static` does not mean the value lives forever. An owned `String` satisfies the bound and is still dropped at the end of its owner's scope. The bound only says the receiver may keep the value as long as it likes, because nothing inside it can dangle. `thread::spawn` puts this bound on its closure (lesson 10).

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: The dot product: one number that measures alignment
md: A dot product of 0 does not mean the vectors are unrelated in every sense; it means they are **perpendicular** (orthogonal). And a big dot product does not by itself mean similar direction: it can come from long vectors. When you want direction only, normalize first or use cosine.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Orthogonality, projections and least squares
md: Orthogonal matrices keep lengths and angles, and $Q^{-1} = Q^\top$. Projecting $\mathbf{b}$ onto a line or a column space leaves a residual orthogonal to it, and that orthogonality condition, $X^\top(\mathbf{y} - X\mathbf{w}) = \mathbf{0}$, is least squares.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Loss: turning "fits the data" into one number
md: The loss you minimize is computed on the **training** data, but what you actually care about is performance on new data. Lessons 6 to 9 show how these two come apart, and what to do about it.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Overfitting: when the training loss lies
md: Zero training error is not proof of a good model, and not proof of a bad one either. The degree-9 fit has zero training error and poor test error; lesson 9 shows that large modern networks can also hit zero training error and still generalize.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Data pitfalls: leakage, distribution shift and baselines
md: Fit everything (scalers, feature selection, imputation) inside the training fold, ideally with a Pipeline. Split by group or by time when rows are related. Expect distribution shift in deployment, and always report a trivial baseline next to your model.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Multi-class outputs: softmax, logits and the p minus y gradient
md: Misconception: raising one logit only raises its own probability. The Jacobian's off-diagonal entries $-p_i p_j$ are negative, so every other probability falls (they must still sum to 1). That is why a wrong class's logit gets the positive gradient $p_j$ even though the loss $-\ln p_y$ reads only the true class: $p_y$ depends on every logit through the softmax denominator.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Processes and limited direct execution
md: A system call is not just a function call. It looks like one because the C library wraps it, but inside is a trap that changes privilege level, and the kernel, not the caller, decides which code runs.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Waiting for something: condition variables and semaphores
md: A condition variable has no memory: signaling when nobody waits does nothing. That is why the waiting thread must check a state variable before it sleeps, rather than relying on catching the signal.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Describing data: mean, median, percentiles and outliers
md: Percentiles do not average. The p99 of two servers combined is not the mean of their two p99 values: it depends on how many requests each served and on the shape of both tails. Compute percentiles from the merged raw data (or from merged histograms).

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Continuous variables: densities, CDFs and common distributions
md: A density value is not a probability. A density of 2 does not mean probability 2, and the probability of any single exact value is 0, which is why $<$ and $\le$ give the same answer for continuous variables.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Bayesian estimation: priors, posteriors and MAP
md: Prior plus data gives a posterior. MAP is maximum likelihood plus a log-prior term, which is why L2 and L1 penalties are Gaussian and Laplace priors in disguise.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Fixed budget, best split: IsoFLOP curves
md: Compute-optimal training scales model size and data **together**, each roughly as the square root of compute. The rule of thumb that falls out is about 20 training tokens per parameter.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Building your own test set: queries, guidelines, pools and LLM judges
md: Never compare an LLM-based system against others using labels from the same or a similar LLM without a human check. Thomas et al. warn that LLM labels may favor rankers that themselves use LLMs. Before trusting LLM labels, have humans judge a sample that includes that system's results, and report the kappa. Judge biases, circularity and safe deployment are covered in *LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling*.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Measuring two real systems on SciFact: tests, intervals, pool bias
md: Simplified: this treats SciFact's qrels as the truth, but they are not exhaustive either, so an abstract outside them may still be relevant. The experiment shows the direction and size of pool bias for systems missing from the pool, not exact true scores.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: Lab: train a tiny encoder with in-batch negatives and measure it
md: Always run BM25 on the same queries before you celebrate a dense model. A trained encoder that loses to a 1994 formula on your data is common, and you only find out by measuring both.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Training BPE: count adjacent pairs, merge the top one, repeat
md: Ties are common on small data. This code picks the pair it encountered first, so a different tie-break or a different word order can produce a different merge list. Real trainers fix a deterministic rule; production implementations also update pair counts incrementally instead of recounting everything, as Sennrich et al. note.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: WordPiece, Unigram and SentencePiece in depth
md: BPE replays merges in learned order. WordPiece scores merges by count(ab) / (count(a) count(b)) and encodes by longest match. Unigram prunes a big vocabulary by likelihood and segments with Viterbi. SentencePiece runs BPE or Unigram on raw text with the space as a symbol.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Batch size, gradient accumulation and tuning hyperparameters
md: Batch size sets the speed; the learning rate decides whether you train at all. Tune the learning rate first, on a log scale: a range test finds the decade, random trials refine it. When you accumulate gradients, divide each micro-batch loss by the number of micro-batches.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: HNSW, IVF, PQ and production indexes
lessonTitle: IVF: clustering the space, nlist and nprobe
md: IVF costs about nlist + nprobe x N/nlist distances per query. nprobe is the query-time knob, like ef in HNSW: each extra probe opens one more cell and catches neighbors that sit across a boundary, at a cost roughly proportional to the extra vectors scanned.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Install scripts: why installing a package runs its code
md: Blocking install scripts stops code that runs at install time. It does not stop malicious code that runs when your app imports the package, or a `.pth` file that Python runs on start-up. It removes the easiest path, not every path.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: When a dependency is compromised: a response playbook
md: Malicious dependency equals intrusion. Scope by version and time window, contain, assume every machine that ran it is compromised, rotate secrets from a clean machine, hunt, rebuild, then fix the control that failed.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Verification is the fix: why filtered self-training does not collapse
md: The generator does not have to be right; the kept set has to be. Collapse is avoided when a verifier keeps more correct than incorrect examples, and its judgments must track this generator's actual errors.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: mmap: putting a file into your address space
md: `mmap` signals failure with `MAP_FAILED`, which is `(void *) -1`, not `NULL`. Code that checks `if (p == NULL)` misses every error and later dereferences address -1.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: When mmap wins, when it hurts, and how to steer it
md: `MAP_FIXED` forcibly replaces whatever is already mapped at that address. In a multithreaded program another thread (or a library calling `dlopen`, which loads a shared library at run time, or `malloc`) may have just mapped something there, and you silently destroy it. mmap(2) recommends `MAP_FIXED_NOREPLACE`, which fails with `EEXIST` (already exists) instead of clobbering.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: SS7: a signalling club that stopped being a club
md: The common mistake is to look for a bug to patch. SS7 location tracking and SMS redirection use messages exactly as specified. The fix is deciding who may send which message about which subscriber, at the network edge.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: SIM swaps and port-outs: an identity problem, not a radio problem
md: A phone number is an account at someone else's company. Carriers must verify people before moving numbers; everyone else should treat a recent SIM change as a red flag and stop letting SMS alone prove identity.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a telecom and space defence map
md: Telecom and space systems fail in the same way: trust given to whoever can reach an interface. Bind every claim to an authenticated peer, check that requests make sense for their subject, encrypt hops you do not control, and audit what the system really does.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Two ways to spend more compute on one prompt
md: Test-time compute is not free at serving time. Every extra sample or thinking token is paid on every request, by every user. Training compute is paid once. That asymmetry decides when test-time scaling is worth it.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Thinking longer: reasoning models and budget forcing
md: Thinking longer does not scale forever. s1's gains flattened after about six forced continuations, suppressing the stop too often led to repetitive loops, and the context window (the most tokens the model can read and write in one pass) caps how long one trace can be. Parallel methods (voting, PRM search over several traces) can extend scaling past that point; s1 found they complement sequential scaling.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: Build a TTT-Linear layer: inner loop, dual form and outer gradient
